replacement: “Well, this is how it was,” Mr. Enfield answered. “I was coming home from some place at the end of the world, at about three o’clock on a black winter morning. My way led through a part of town where there was literally nothing to see but lamps. Street after street, with everyone asleep—street after street, all lit up as if for a procession and all as empty as a church—until at last I got into the state of mind where a man listens and listens and starts to long for the sight of a policeman. All at once I saw two figures. One was a little man stumping along eastward at a good pace, and the other was a girl of maybe eight or ten, running as hard as she could down a cross street. Well, sir, the two ran into each other at the corner, naturally enough. And then came the horrible part of it, for the man calmly trampled over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground. It sounds like nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man. It was like some damned Juggernaut. I let out a few halloas, took to my heels, grabbed my gentleman by the collar, and brought him back to where quite a group had already gathered around the screaming child. He was perfectly cool and put up no resistance, but he gave me one look, so ugly that it brought the sweat out on me as if I’d been running. The people who had turned out were the girl’s own family, and soon the doctor arrived, the one she had been sent for. Well, the child was not much the worse—more frightened than hurt, according to the Sawbones—and you might have supposed that would be the end of it. But there was one curious circumstance. I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight. So had the child’s family, which was only natural. But it was the doctor who struck me. He was the usual cut-and-dried apothecary, of no particular age or colour, with a strong Edinburgh accent and about as emotional as a bagpipe. Well, sir, he was like the rest of us. Every time he looked at my prisoner, I saw that Sawbones turn sick and white with the wish to kill him. I knew what was in his mind, just as he knew what was in mine. Since killing was out of the question, we did the next best thing. We told the man we could and would make such a scandal of this that his name would stink from one end of London to the other. If he had any friends or any credit, we promised him he would lose them. And all the time, as we were piling it on red hot, we were keeping the women off him as well as we could, for they were as wild as harpies. I never saw such a circle of hateful faces. And there was the man in the middle, with a kind of black, sneering coolness—frightened too, I could see that—but carrying it off, sir, really like Satan. ‘If you choose to make capital out of this accident,’ said he, ‘I am naturally helpless. No gentleman wants a scene,’ says he. ‘Name your figure.’ Well, we screwed him up to a hundred pounds for the child’s family. He clearly would have liked to hold out, but there was something about the lot of us that meant mischief, and at last he gave in. The next thing was to get the money, and where do you think he took us but to that place with the door? He whipped out a key, went in, and soon came back with ten pounds or so in gold and a cheque for the rest, on Coutts’s, made payable to bearer and signed with a name I can’t mention, though it is one of the points of my story. It was a name, at least, that is very well known and often printed. The sum was steep, but the signature was good for more than that, if it was genuine. I took the liberty of pointing out to my gentleman that the whole business looked suspect, and that in real life a man doesn’t walk into a cellar door at four in the morning and come out with another man’s cheque for close on a hundred pounds. But he was quite easy and sneering. ‘Set your mind at rest,’ says he. ‘I will stay with you until the banks open and cash the cheque myself.’ So off we all went—the doctor, the child’s father, our friend and myself—and we spent the rest of the night in my chambers. Next day, when we had breakfasted, we went in a body to the bank. I handed in the cheque myself and said I had every reason to believe it was a forgery. Not a bit of it. The cheque was genuine.”
“In return,” said Mr. Utterson, “will you do me a favour?”

Late that afternoon Mr. Utterson called at Dr. Jekyll’s door, where Poole let him in at once. The butler took him through the kitchen quarters and over a yard that had once been a garden, to the building people called, without much distinction, the laboratory or the dissecting-rooms. The doctor had bought the house from the heirs of a famous surgeon. Since his own tastes were chemical rather than anatomical, he had put the block at the bottom of the garden to a different use. The lawyer had never before been admitted to this part of his friend’s premises. He studied the dingy, windowless building with curiosity, and as he crossed the theatre he felt an uneasy strangeness all around him. Eager students had once packed the place; now it lay gaunt and silent. The tables were loaded with chemical apparatus, crates stood about, packing straw littered the floor, and a dim light came down through the foggy dome. At the far end, a flight of stairs rose to a door covered in red baize, and through it Mr. Utterson was at last shown into the doctor’s study. It was a large room, lined with glass cupboards and furnished, among other things, with a full-length mirror and a business table. Three dusty, iron-barred windows looked out on the court. A fire was burning in the grate, and a lit lamp stood on the mantelpiece, since the fog was already thickening even inside the houses. Close up to the warmth sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly sick. He did not rise to greet his visitor. He held out a cold hand instead, and bade him welcome in a voice that had changed.
“And by every account a very odd man to write it,” added the lawyer.
“Foul play!” cried the lawyer, who was a good deal alarmed and, in consequence, rather inclined to be irritable. “What foul play! What does the man mean?”
“It seems very much altered,” replied the lawyer, very pale, but meeting his gaze.

The besiegers, appalled by their own uproar and by the silence that followed it, drew back a little and looked in. The study lay before them in the quiet lamplight. A good fire glowed and crackled on the hearth, the kettle sang its thin song, a drawer or two stood open, papers were set out neatly on the business table, and nearer the fire the tea things were laid. It was the quietest room you could imagine, and, apart from the glass cupboards full of chemicals, the most ordinary in London that night.

That drew them to the fireside, where the easy-chair had been pulled snugly up and the tea things stood ready at the sitter’s elbow, with the sugar already in the cup. There were several books on a shelf, and one lay open beside the tea things. Utterson was amazed to find it was a copy of a pious work that Jekyll had several times said he greatly esteemed—and it was annotated, in his own hand, with startling blasphemies.
